analysis.one_liner: Repeals the fossil fuel tax breaks enacted in the 2005 Energy Policy Act.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2005 Energy Policy Act included a package of special tax breaks for producing fossil fuels. This bill would erase those tax breaks entirely, treating them as if they had never been enacted. Repealing them would mean oil, gas, and coal companies paid more in taxes, with the revenue effectively returning to the Treasury.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers as a whole benefit, because tax breaks for fossil fuel producers would end, and no other taxpayer group would be asked to make up the difference elsewhere in the bill. Ordinary people also gain only indirectly: the cost of fossil fuel tax incentives is spread across everyone who pays taxes, while the direct benefits flow to a concentrated set of energy companies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals subtitle B of title XIII of the Energy Policy Act of 2005, the provisions creating energy tax incentives for fossil fuel production, and directs that the tax code be applied as if they had never been enacted.

Because the repeal applies retroactively, as if the 2005 provisions were never part of the law, the special tax treatment for fossil fuel producers would be erased rather than merely ended for future projects.
The bill carried no other provisions: it raised no taxes on households and made no changes beyond removing the fossil fuel incentives, so no ordinary taxpayer group bore a new cost under its text.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal producers, along with companies operating natural gas pipelines and petroleum refineries, would bear the cost of losing the special tax incentives they received under the 2005 energy law. Those companies' subjects include depletion allowances, depreciation rules, and refining tax provisions, which are the mechanisms the repealed subtitle covered. Any portion of the lost tax advantages that companies passed to consumers through prices would be a secondary cost for energy users.

drawbacks.text: Repealing tax breaks for energy producers could reduce investment in domestic oil, gas, and coal production, and companies would likely try to pass some of the added tax burden to consumers through higher energy prices.
The repeal is written to apply as if the 2005 provisions had never existed, meaning companies that had made decisions or investments in reliance on those incentives would lose them retroactively.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had a straightforward design: remove the fossil fuel tax incentives and nothing else, so the benefits to taxpayers through forgone industry tax breaks are not offset by new spending or tax increases elsewhere. The main cost is the risk of modestly higher energy prices or reduced energy investment, which energy companies would spread across consumers. On its face, the trade favors taxpayers, but the bill never advanced far enough for its economic effects to be examined in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: Biden introduced the bill, the Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, and it sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Biden introduced the bill on May 11, 2006, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No cosponsors signed on to the bill, which was introduced with only its sponsor's support.

The committee took no further action: the bill's entire recorded history consists of its introduction and referral, and it never reached the Senate floor for a vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and related energy companies are better off because the bill died: they kept the tax incentives the 2005 Energy Policy Act had given them, since the repeal never moved past committee. Taxpayers did not receive the revenue that repeal would have preserved.

for.name: Sen. Joseph R. Biden, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the fossil fuel tax incentives in the 2005 Energy Policy Act; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its history.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled committee action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no recorded support or opposition beyond its Democratic sponsor; it never came to a vote, so no party breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed the tax incentives for fossil fuel production that the 2005 Energy Policy Act gave these companies, including expanded depletion allowances and related depreciation benefits. Those breaks reduce what the companies owe in taxes at public expense.

Coal production incentives in the 2005 law's tax package, including credits for advanced coal projects, would have been repealed. Coal companies would have paid more in taxes, and the public subsidy supporting their fuel would have ended.

industries.industry: Natural gas pipeline and petroleum refining companies
industries.note: The bill's subjects include depreciation rules and provisions for gas pipelines and petroleum refineries, tax benefits that would have been wiped out by the repeal. These companies would have lost accelerated write-offs that lowered their tax bills.
